metadata.title: A Simple Unpredictable Pseudo-Random Number Generator
metadata.authors: L. Blum, M. Blum, M. Shub
metadata.venue: SIAM J. Comput., Vol. 15, No. 2, May 1986, pp. 364-383
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Seed domain
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a set of positive integers (parameter values), and for each $N \in \mathcal{N}$ let $X_N \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ be a set of seeds. The set $X = \{(N,x) \mid N \in \mathcal{N},\, x \in X_N\}$ is called a seed domain.
nodes.statement_clean: A seed domain pairs each parameter value with its admissible seeds.

nodes.name: Accessible probability distribution and seed space
nodes.statement: An ensemble $U = \{\mu_n\}$ on $X^n = \{(N,x)\in X : |N|=n\}$ is accessible if some probabilistic poly($n$)-time procedure samples $\mu_n$ with negligible error. The pair $(X,U)$ is a seed space.
nodes.statement_clean: Seed space = a seed domain together with an efficiently sampleable probability distribution on seeds of each length.

nodes.name: Pseudo-random sequence generator
nodes.statement: A (base $b$) pseudo-random sequence generator $G$ on seed space $X$ is an effective map $G: X \to \Sigma^\infty$ such that for each $s \geq 0$ there is $t \geq 0$ with: for all $(N,x) \in X$ with $\mu_n(N,x) > 0$, the initial $n^s$ digits of $G(N,x)$ are output in time $O(n^t)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A PRG produces, in polynomial time and from short seeds, long output sequences over the base-$b$ alphabet.

nodes.name: Transformation, partition, and (X,T,B) generator
nodes.statement: A transformation $T:X\to X$ is a poly-time effective map preserving $\mu_n$. A partition $B:X\to \Sigma$ is a poly-time effective map. The triple $(X,T,B)$ defines a PRG by $[G(N,x)]_k = B(T^k x)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A structured PRG = a measure-preserving transformation $T$ on the seed space plus a poly-time partition $B$ that reads off one output symbol per orbit step.

nodes.name: $1/P$ generator (base $b$)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N} = \{P>1 : \gcd(P,b)=1\}$ and seed domain $X = \bigsqcup_{P\in\mathcal{N}} \mathbb{Z}_P^*$. Define $G(r/P) = .q_1 q_2 q_3 \ldots$ as the base-$b$ quotient digits of $r/P$. Equivalently $T(r) = br \bmod P$ on $\mathbb{Z}_P^*$ and $B(r) = \lfloor br/P \rfloor$.
nodes.statement_clean: The $1/P$ generator outputs the successive base-$b$ quotient digits of $r/P$.

nodes.name: $x^2 \bmod N$ generator
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N} = \{N = P\cdot Q : P,Q \text{ distinct equal-length primes} \equiv 3 \bmod 4\}$. For $N\in\mathcal{N}$, $X_N = QR_N = \{x^2 \bmod N : x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*\}$. Define $T(x) = x^2 \bmod N$ and $B(x) = \mathrm{parity}(x)$. The output bit-sequence is $b_0 b_1 \ldots$ with $b_i = \mathrm{parity}(x_i)$, $x_{i+1} = x_i^2 \bmod N$.
nodes.statement_clean: The $x^2 \bmod N$ generator iterates squaring on quadratic residues modulo $N=PQ$ ($P,Q\equiv 3 \bmod 4$) and outputs the parity bit of each iterate.

nodes.name: Generalized de Bruijn sequence
nodes.statement: A (generalized) de Bruijn sequence of period $P-1$, base $b$, is a $b$-ary sequence of period $P-1$ such that (1) every $b$-ary string of length $|P|-1$ occurs at least once, and (2) every $b$-ary string of length $|P|$ occurs at most once in any period.
nodes.statement_clean: A maximum-length-like base-$b$ sequence whose substrings of length $|P|-1$ all appear and whose substrings of length $|P|$ each appear at most once per period.

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-advantage for guessing parity
nodes.statement: A 0-1 valued probabilistic poly-time procedure $P(\cdot,\cdot)$ has an $\epsilon$-advantage for $N$ in guessing $\mathrm{parity}(x_{-1})$ given $x_0 \in QR_N$ iff $\sum_{x_0\in QR_N} \mathrm{Prob}[P[N,x_0]=\mathrm{parity}(x_{-1})] / (\varphi(N)/4) \geq 1/2 + \epsilon$.
nodes.statement_clean: The procedure beats a fair coin by $\epsilon$ in predicting the parity of the previous iterate.

nodes.name: Predictor and $\epsilon$-advantage to the left
nodes.statement: A predictor $P(\cdot,\cdot)$ is a probabilistic poly-time procedure that, given $N$ and $b_1\ldots b_k$ (with $k \leq \mathrm{poly}(|N|)$), outputs a bit. $P$ has an $\epsilon$-advantage for $N$ in predicting to the left iff for some $k$, $\sum_{x\in QR_N} \mathrm{Prob}[P(N,b_1(x),\ldots,b_k(x)) = b_0(x)]/(\varphi(N)/4) \geq 1/2 + \epsilon$, where $b_i(x) = \mathrm{parity}(x^{2^i} \bmod N)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A left-predictor tries to guess the bit just before a window of generator outputs; $\epsilon$-advantage means it beats a fair coin by $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Carmichael's $\lambda$-function
nodes.statement: For $M = 2^e p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$ with distinct odd primes $p_i$: $\lambda(2^e) = 2^{e-2}$ if $e \geq 3$ and $2^{e-1}$ if $e=1,2$, and $\lambda(M) = \mathrm{lcm}[\lambda(2^e), (p_1-1)p_1^{e_1-1}, \ldots, (p_k-1)p_k^{e_k-1}]$.
nodes.statement_clean: $\lambda(M)$ is the exponent of the multiplicative group $\mathbb{Z}_M^*$.

nodes.name: Special prime; special number of the prescribed form
nodes.statement: A prime $P$ is special if $P = 2P_1+1$ and $P_1 = 2P_2+1$ where $P_1,P_2$ are odd primes. $N = PQ$ is a special number of the prescribed form if $P,Q$ are distinct special primes with $P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ and $P_2 \neq Q_2$.
nodes.statement_clean: A special prime sits at the top of a length-3 Sophie-Germain-style chain; a special $N$ is the product of two such primes congruent to $3 \bmod 4$.

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm assumption
nodes.statement: For any procedure $P[b,P,y]$ solving discrete log, any constant $0<\delta<1$, integer $t$, polynomial $\mathrm{poly}$: for all sufficiently large $n$ and all but a $\delta$-fraction of $n$-bit primes $P$, for all primitive roots $b \bmod P$, $\mathrm{Prob}\{\text{expected time of } P[b,P,y] \geq \mathrm{poly}(n) \mid y \sim \mathbb{Z}_P^*\} > 1/n^t$.
nodes.statement_clean: Discrete log is intractable on most inputs.

nodes.name: Quadratic residuacity assumption (QRA)
nodes.statement: For any probabilistic poly-time $P[N,x]$ outputting 0 or 1, any $0<\delta<1$ and integer $t$: for $n$ sufficiently large and all but a $\delta$-fraction of $n$-bit $N = PQ$ (distinct equal-length odd primes), the probability that $P[N,x]$ guesses quadratic residuacity incorrectly (for $x$ uniform in $\mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$) exceeds $1/n^t$.
nodes.statement_clean: No efficient procedure decides quadratic residuacity correctly on most $N$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$.

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm (index finding) problem
nodes.statement: Given a prime $P$, a primitive root $b$ mod $P$, and $y \in \mathbb{Z}_P^*$, find $x \in \mathbb{Z}_P^*$ such that $b^x \bmod P = y$.
nodes.statement_clean: Compute the discrete log of $y$ to base $b$ modulo $P$.

nodes.name: Quadratic residuacity problem
nodes.statement: Given $N$, a product of two distinct odd primes, and $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$ (Jacobi symbol $+1$), decide whether $x$ is a quadratic residue mod $N$.
nodes.statement_clean: Decide quadratic residuacity of $x$ mod $N$ when $x$ has Jacobi symbol $+1$.

nodes.name: $1/P$ generator yields generalized de Bruijn sequences
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be prime, $b \in \{1,\ldots,P-1\}$ a primitive root mod $P$, and $r_0 \in \{1,\ldots,P-1\}$. Then the sequence generated by the $1/P$ generator (base $b$) with input $r_0/P$ is a generalized de Bruijn sequence of period $P-1$ base $b$.
nodes.statement_clean: When $b$ is a primitive root mod prime $P$, the $1/P$ generator outputs a generalized de Bruijn sequence.
conclusions: The output sequence is a generalized de Bruijn sequence of period $P-1$, base $b$.

nodes.name: $1/P$ generator is predictable (4 inference problems)
nodes.statement: Let $P,b$ relatively prime integers $>1$ and $0 < r_0 < P$. Problems 1-4 (extending remainders, recovering $r_m$ from $|P|$ digits, recovering $P$ from $r_m, r_{m+1}$, and recovering $P$ from $\lceil \log_b(2P^2)\rceil$ digits via continued fractions) are all solvable in polynomial time in $|P|$.
nodes.statement_clean: Four poly-time inference algorithms show the $1/P$ generator is fully predictable from short observations.
conclusions: Problems 1-4 (predicting/extending the sequence and recovering $P$) are all poly($|P|$)-time solvable.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2 (predictability of $1/P$ generator)
nodes.statement: Solve each problem in turn: (P1) compute $r_{m\pm k} = b^{\pm k} r_m \bmod P$ and read off quotient digits; (P2) recover $r_m$ from $|P|$ quotient digits by truncation; (P3) recover $P$ as the unique value in $\{(b r_m - r_{m+1})/i\}_{i=1}^{b-1}$ coprime to $1,\ldots,b$; (P4) recover $P$ from $\lceil \log_b(2P^2)\rceil$ quotient digits via continued-fraction convergents.

nodes.name: Solve Problem 1 (extend remainders)
nodes.statement: $r_{m+k} = b^k r_m \bmod P$ and $r_{m-1} = b^{-1} r_m \bmod P$, where $b^{-1}$ is the inverse of $b$ mod $P$. Then $q_{m+1}\ldots q_{m+k} = \lfloor (b^k r_m)/P \rfloor$.

nodes.name: Solve Problem 2 (recover $r_m$ from quotient digits)
nodes.statement: By (6), $r_m = (q_{m+1}\ldots q_{m+|P|}) \cdot P/b^{|P|} + r_{m+|P|}/b^{|P|}$. Since $r_{m+|P|} < P < b^{|P|}$, $r_m = \lfloor (q_{m+1}\ldots q_{m+|P|}) \cdot P / b^{|P|} \rfloor$.

nodes.name: Solve Problem 3 (recover $P$ from $r_m, r_{m+1}$)
nodes.statement: $b r_m = r_{m+1} + q_{m+1} P$ with $0 < q_{m+1} < b$. So $P \in \{(b r_m - r_{m+1})/i : i=1,\ldots,b-1\}$; pick the unique $P$ coprime to $1,\ldots,b$ (uniqueness via $\gcd$ argument).

nodes.name: Solve Problem 4 (recover $P$ via continued fractions)
nodes.statement: By (6), $r_m/P = .q_{m+1}\ldots q_{m+k}/b^k + e$ with $0 \leq e < 1/b^k$. By LeVeque Thm. 9.10, when $1/b^k \leq 1/(2P^2)$ (i.e. $\log_b(2P^2) \leq k$), $r_m/P$ is a convergent of the continued fraction of $.q_{m+1}\ldots q_{m+k}/b^k$. Generate convergents $A_i/B_i$ until the first $k$ digits of $A_i/B_i$ match the input; then $r_m=A_i$, $P = B_i$.

nodes.name: Unique-quadratic-residue square root for $P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$
nodes.statement: If $N = PQ$ with $P,Q$ distinct primes $P \equiv Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$, then each quadratic residue mod $N$ has exactly one square root that is itself a quadratic residue mod $N$.
nodes.statement_clean: When $P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$, exactly one of the four square roots of a quadratic residue is again a quadratic residue.
conclusions: Each quadratic residue mod $N$ has exactly one square root that is a quadratic residue.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: A quadratic residue mod $N$ has four square roots $\pm x, \pm y$. Since $N \equiv 1 \bmod 4$, $(\pm x/N) = (-x/N)$ similarly for $y$. Since $P \equiv 3 \bmod 4$, $(x/N) \neq (y/N)$. Drop the two roots with Jacobi symbol $-1$; of the remaining $\pm x$, exactly one has Jacobi $+1$ w.r.t. both $P$ and $Q$ (since $P \equiv 3 \bmod 4$), and that one is the unique quadratic residue.

nodes.name: Parity-guessing advantage converts to QR-guessing advantage
nodes.statement: An $\epsilon$-advantage for guessing $\mathrm{parity}(x_{-1})$ given quadratic residue $x_0$ can be converted, efficiently and uniformly, to an $\epsilon$-advantage for guessing quadratic residuacity of $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Predicting the previous parity is at least as hard as deciding quadratic residuacity.
assumptions: $\epsilon$-advantage procedure for parity of $x_{-1}$ given $x_0 \in QR_N$
conclusions: An $\epsilon$-advantage procedure for quadratic residuacity of $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Given $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$, set $x_0 = x^2 \bmod N$. The two square roots of $x_0$ in $\mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$ are $x$ and $N-x$, of opposite parity since $N$ is odd. Only one of these (namely $x_{-1}$) is a quadratic residue, and only one has parity equal to $\mathrm{parity}(x_{-1})$. So $x \in QR_N$ iff $\mathrm{parity}(x) = \mathrm{parity}(x_{-1})$.

nodes.name: Amplification of QR-guessing advantage (Goldwasser-Micali)
nodes.statement: An $\epsilon$-advantage for guessing quadratic residuacity can be amplified to a $1/2-\epsilon'$ advantage, uniformly and efficiently.
nodes.statement_clean: Any nonneglible advantage in deciding quadratic residuacity can be amplified close to certainty.
conclusions: A $1/2 - \epsilon'$ advantage procedure for quadratic residuacity.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: Sample uniformly from $QR_N$ and from $\mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1) - QR_N$; estimate $A,B$ with $A - B \geq 2\epsilon$. Given $x$, randomize via $x \cdot r^2 \bmod N$ to make $x \cdot r^2$ uniform on $QR_N$ (resp. $\mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)-QR_N$) when $x \in QR_N$ (resp. not), then test repeatedly and compare the empirical fraction to $A,B$.

nodes.name: Backwards algorithm: efficient backwards generation given factorization
nodes.statement: There is an efficient deterministic algorithm $A$ which, given $N$ of the prescribed form, the prime factors of $N$, and any quadratic residue $x_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*$, computes the unique quadratic residue $x_{-1} \bmod N$ such that $(x_{-1})^2 \bmod N = x_0$.
nodes.statement_clean: Knowing $P,Q$ lets you efficiently invert the squaring map on quadratic residues.
assumptions: $N = PQ$ of the prescribed form ($P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ distinct equal-length primes)
conclusions: $A$ outputs the unique $x_{-1} \in QR_N$ with $x_{-1}^2 \equiv x_0 \bmod N$, in poly time.

nodes.name: Backwards-jump algorithm $A(P,Q,x_0) = x_{-1}$
nodes.statement: Given primes $P,Q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$ and $x_0 \in QR_N$ with $N=PQ$, computes $x_{-1} \in QR_N$ with $x_{-1}^2 \equiv x_0$ via Tonelli (using $P+1/4$) plus Chinese Remainder.
output: Quadratic residue $x_{-1} \bmod N$ such that $x_{-1}^2 \equiv x_0 \bmod N$
nodes.pseudocode:
1. Compute $x_P = x_0^{(P+1)/4} \bmod P$ such that $(x_P/P)=+1$.
2. Compute $x_Q = x_0^{(Q+1)/4} \bmod Q$ similarly.
3. Use Euclidean algorithm to find $u,v$ with $Pu + Qv = 1$.
4. Output $x_{-1} = x_P \cdot Q v + x_Q \cdot P u \bmod N$ (the unique square root of $x_0$ that is a quadratic residue mod $N$).

nodes.name: Compute square root mod $P$
nodes.statement: $x_P = x_0^{(P+1)/4} \bmod P$, choosing the value with $(x_P/P) = +1$ (works because $P \equiv 3 \bmod 4$).

nodes.name: Compute square root mod $Q$
nodes.statement: $x_Q = x_0^{(Q+1)/4} \bmod Q$, choosing the QR root mod $Q$.

nodes.name: Combine via CRT
nodes.statement: Find $u,v$ with $Pu + Qv = 1$ via Euclidean algorithm. Output $x_{-1} = x_P \cdot Q v + x_Q \cdot P u \bmod N$.

nodes.name: $x^2 \bmod N$ generator is poly-time unpredictable to the left (modulo QRA)
nodes.statement: Modulo the QRA, the $x^2 \bmod N$ generator is an unpredictable cryptographically secure PRG. For each probabilistic poly-time predictor $P$, constant $0 < \delta < 1$, and integer $t$, $P$ has at most $1/n^t$ advantage in predicting to the left (for sufficiently large $n$ and all but a $\delta$-fraction of prescribed $N$ of length $n$).
nodes.statement_clean: Under QRA, no efficient algorithm can predict the bit before any window of generator outputs with non-negligible advantage.
conclusions: For every poly-time predictor $P$, every $\delta \in (0,1)$, and every integer $t$: $P$'s advantage to the left is $\leq 1/n^t$ on all but a $\delta$-fraction of prescribed $N$ of length $n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Given a left-predictor with $\epsilon$-advantage for $N$, generate $b_0 b_1 \ldots$ from seed $x_0$; then $\mathrm{parity}(x_{-1}) = b_{-1}$, yielding an $\epsilon$-advantage for parity. By Lemma 2 convert to a quadratic-residuacity guesser; by Lemma 3 amplify to $1/2 - 1/n^t$, contradicting the QRA.

nodes.name: $x^2 \bmod N$ sequences pass every poly-time statistical test (modulo QRA)
nodes.statement: Modulo the QRA, the sequences produced by the $x^2 \bmod N$ generator pass every probabilistic polynomial-time statistical test.
nodes.statement_clean: Under QRA, no poly-time test can distinguish the generator's output from truly random bits with non-negligible advantage.
conclusions: The $x^2 \bmod N$ generator passes every probabilistic poly-time statistical test (in the sense of Yao).

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 5 (following Yao)
nodes.statement: If a test $T$ distinguishes pseudo-random and random sequences with advantage at $1/n^t$, find indices $j,k$ such that $T$'s expected value on $r_1\ldots r_j b_{j+1} \ldots b_{j+k+1}$ differs by $1/(n^{t+1}\cdot \mathrm{poly}_1(n))$ from its value on $r_1\ldots r_{j+1} b_{j+2} \ldots b_{j+k+1}$, then convert into a predictor for $b_0$ using a biased coin whose bias depends on the empirical $a^0 - a^1$.

nodes.name: Modified $x^2 \bmod N$ generator using location bit
nodes.statement: The modified $x^2 \bmod N$ generator extracting the location bit ($\mathrm{location}(x) = 0$ if $x < (N-1)/2$, else $1$) at each stage (instead of parity) is also cryptographically secure modulo the QRA.

nodes.name: Two-bit modified generator security conjecture
nodes.statement: The modified $x^2 \bmod N$ generator extracting two bits per stage, $\mathrm{parity}(x)$ and $\mathrm{location}(x)$, is cryptographically secure.

nodes.name: How many bits per stage retain cryptographic security?
nodes.statement: Parity is the least significant bit and location is morally the most significant bit. How many bits (and which ones) can we extract at each stage and still maintain cryptographic security?

nodes.name: Period of $x^2 \bmod N$ sequence divides $\lambda(\lambda(N))$
nodes.statement: Let $N=PQ$ of prescribed form, $x_0$ a quadratic residue mod $N$, $\pi = \pi(x_0)$ the period of the sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots$. Then $\pi \mid \lambda(\lambda(N))$.
nodes.statement_clean: The orbit length under squaring divides $\lambda(\lambda(N))$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement: For $x \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*(+1)$ the order of $x$ is odd. By Carmichael's extension of Euler's theorem, $2^{\lambda(\mathrm{ord}_N x)} \equiv 1 \bmod (\mathrm{ord}_N x_0)$, and $\pi$ is the least positive integer with $2^\pi \equiv 1 \bmod (\mathrm{ord}_N x_0)$, so $\pi \mid \lambda(\mathrm{ord}_N x_0) \mid \lambda(\lambda(N))$.

nodes.name: Conditions ensuring $\pi(x_0) = \lambda(\lambda(N))$
nodes.statement: If (1) $\mathrm{ord}_{\lambda(N)/2}(2) = \lambda(\lambda(N))$ and (2) $\mathrm{ord}_N(x_0) = \lambda(N)/2$, then $\lambda(\lambda(N)) \mid \pi(x_0)$ (and combined with Theorem 6, equality holds).
nodes.statement_clean: Under two order conditions, the orbit length equals $\lambda(\lambda(N))$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: $\pi$ is the least positive integer with $x_0^{2^\pi} \equiv x_0 \bmod N$. Since $\mathrm{ord}_N(x_0) = \lambda(N)/2$, $2^\pi \equiv 1 \bmod (\lambda(N)/2)$, so $\lambda(\lambda(N)) \mid \pi$.

nodes.name: Special-$N$ sufficient condition for $\mathrm{ord}_{\lambda(N)/2}(2) = \lambda(\lambda(N))$
nodes.statement: Suppose $N$ is a special number of the prescribed form and 2 is a quadratic residue with respect to at most one of $P_1, Q_1$. Then $\mathrm{ord}_{\lambda(N)/2}(2) = \lambda(\lambda(N))$ (and so $\lambda(\lambda(N)) = \pi(x_0)$ for some $x_0$).
nodes.statement_clean: For most special $N$, condition (1) of Theorem 7 holds.
assumptions: $N$ is a special number of the prescribed form
2 is a quadratic residue w.r.t. at most one of $P_1, Q_1$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement: For $N$ of prescribed form, $\lambda(N) = 2P_1 Q_1$, $\lambda(\lambda(N)) = 2P_2 Q_2$. Argue by cases: if $\mathrm{ord}_{\lambda(N)/2}(2) \mid 2P_2$ or $= P_2 Q_2$, derive contradiction with Fermat's Little Theorem and the QR-of-2 hypothesis.

nodes.name: Period of bit-sequence vs orbit period
nodes.statement: Let $\pi_b(x_0)$ be the period of the bit-sequence $b_0 b_1 \ldots$ produced by the $x^2 \bmod N$ generator. Then $\pi_b(x_0) \mid \pi(x_0)$. What is the exact relation between $\pi_b(x_0)$ and $\pi(x_0)$? Are they generally equal?

nodes.name: Efficient computation of period $\pi(x_0)$
nodes.statement: There is an efficient algorithm $A$ which given $N$ of prescribed form, $\lambda(N)$, $\lambda(\lambda(N))$ AND the factorization of $\lambda(\lambda(N))$, efficiently determines the period $\pi(x_0)$ of any quadratic residue $x_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*$.
nodes.statement_clean: With auxiliary number-theoretic information, the orbit period can be computed efficiently.
assumptions: knowledge of $\lambda(N), \lambda(\lambda(N))$, and the factorization of $\lambda(\lambda(N))$

nodes.name: Period-finding algorithm
nodes.statement: Find the largest $d \mid \lambda(\lambda(N))$ such that $x_0^{2^{\lambda(\lambda(N))/d} \bmod \lambda(N)} \equiv x_0 \bmod N$; then $\pi = \lambda(\lambda(N))/d$.
output: $\pi(x_0)$, the period of the orbit $x_0, x_1, \ldots$

nodes.name: Random-access in forward direction (Theorem 10a)
nodes.statement: There is an efficient deterministic algorithm $A$ such that given $N$, $\lambda(N)$, any quadratic residue $x_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*$, and any positive integer $i$, $A$ efficiently computes $x_i$. Specifically $x_i = x_0^{2^i \bmod \lambda(N)} \bmod N$.
nodes.statement_clean: Knowing $\lambda(N)$ enables jumping forward to the $i$-th iterate in poly time.

nodes.name: Random-access in backward direction (Theorem 10b)
nodes.statement: There is an efficient deterministic algorithm $A$ such that given $N$ of prescribed form, $\lambda(N)$, $x_0 \in QR_N$, and positive integer $i$, $A$ efficiently computes $x_{-i}$.
nodes.statement_clean: $\lambda(N)$ also lets you jump backward by $i$ steps efficiently (using Miller's factoring-from-$\lambda(N)$ result).
conclusions: $A[N, \lambda(N), x_0, i] = x_{-i}$ in poly time.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10b
nodes.statement: Miller has shown how to factor $N=PQ$ given $\lambda(N)$. Then $x_{-i} \bmod P = \pm x_0^{((P+1)/4)^i \bmod (P-1)} \bmod P$ (similar mod $Q$); pick the QR root and use CRT.

nodes.name: Oracle for $(\pi, x_{-i})$ enables factoring
nodes.statement: Let $O$ be an oracle returning $O(N, x_0, i) = (\pi, x_{-i})$. There is an efficient probabilistic algorithm $A^O$ such that $A^O(N) = P$ or $Q$ for $N=PQ$.
nodes.statement_clean: Backwards-jump capability is as hard as factoring.
conclusions: A probabilistic poly-time algorithm $A^O$ outputs a nontrivial factor of $N$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: Search at random for $y \in \mathbb{Z}_N^*$ with $(y/N) = -1$. Set $x_0 = y^2 \bmod N$. Ask oracle for $\pi$ and $x_{-1}$. Then $y^2 \equiv x_{-1}^2 \equiv x_0 \bmod N$ but $y \neq \pm x_{-1}$ (Jacobi mismatch), so $\gcd(y + x_{-1}, N) \in \{P, Q\}$.

nodes.name: Does $x_i$-only oracle enable factoring?
nodes.statement: Can an algorithm use an oracle that outputs just $x_i$, namely $O(N, x_0, i) = x_i$, to factor $N$?

nodes.name: Does period-only oracle enable factoring?
nodes.statement: Can an algorithm use an oracle that outputs just $\pi$, namely $O(N, x_0) = \pi$, to factor $N$?

nodes.name: Pair-guessing security (stronger version of Claim 3)
nodes.statement: For all but a $\delta$-fraction of prescribed $N$, the factors of $N$ are necessary (modulo QRA) to have an $\epsilon$-advantage ($\epsilon \geq 1/|N|^t$) in guessing in poly-time any pair $(\ell, b_\ell)$ ($1 \leq \ell \leq k = \mathrm{poly}(|N|)$), given $N$ and $x_{k+1}$, where $b_\ell = \mathrm{parity}(x_\ell)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Under QRA, no efficient procedure can guess any (location, bit) pair of the generator's output given $N$ and $x_{k+1}$.
conclusions: No probabilistic poly-time procedure guesses $(\ell, b_\ell)$ correctly with advantage $\geq 1/|N|^t$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12
nodes.statement: From a pair-guesser $P$ with $\epsilon$-advantage, build a QR-decider with $\epsilon/\mathrm{poly}(|N|)$-advantage: pick random $\ell \leq \mathrm{poly}(|N|)$, set $x_{\ell+1} = x^2 \bmod N$, generate $x_{k+1}$, run $P[N, x_{k+1}]$; with probability $1/\mathrm{poly}(|N|)$ it returns $(\ell, b)$ for the chosen $\ell$ and $b = \mathrm{parity}(x_\ell)$ tells QR status.

nodes.name: $1/7$ in base 10 is generalized de Bruijn
nodes.statement: With $b=10$, $P=7$, $r=1$: $1/7 = .142857142\ldots$. 10 is a primitive root mod 7, so the period is $7-1=6$. The orbit of $1/7$ under $T$ is $1/7, 3/7, 2/7, 6/7, 4/7, 5/7, 1/7, \ldots$, giving digits $1,4,2,8,5,7,\ldots$.

nodes.name: $x^2 \bmod 133$ generator with seed 4
nodes.statement: Let $N = 7 \cdot 19 = 133$ and $x_0 = 4$. The orbit $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_5 = 4, 16, 123, 100, 25, 93$ has period 6, giving bit-string $0,0,1,0,1,1,\ldots$. Here $\lambda(N) = 18$ and $\lambda(\lambda(N)) = 6$.

nodes.name: $1/503$ in base 10 with continued-fraction recovery
nodes.statement: $P = 503$ is prime and 10 is a primitive root mod 503, giving a period-502 sequence. From any $\lceil \log_{10}(2 \cdot 503^2) \rceil = 6$ consecutive digits (e.g. 433399), the continued-fraction expansion gives convergents whose $5$th convergent $218/503 = .433399\ldots$ matches; hence $P=503$ and $r_m = 218$ are recovered.

nodes.name: Special prime chains and $N = 23 \cdot 47$
nodes.statement: The primes $2879, 1439, 719, 359, 179, 89$ form a special chain. The number $N = 23 \cdot 47$ is a special number of the prescribed form.

nodes.name: Public-key cryptography application (Alice-Bob protocol)
nodes.statement: Alice publishes $N_A = P_A Q_A$ ($P_A, Q_A \equiv 3 \bmod 4$). Bob picks $x_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_{N_A}^*$ at random, sets $x_1 = x_0^2 \bmod N_A$, generates a one-time pad $\bar b = (b_1, \ldots, b_k)$ via the $x^2 \bmod N$ generator with input $(N_A, x_1)$, sends $(\bar m \oplus \bar b, x_{k+1})$. Alice uses her private $P_A, Q_A$ and Theorem 3 to backwards-jump from $x_{k+1}$ to recover $\bar b$ and decrypt.
